title: Variant fallthrough benchmark scratch
content:
Goal: quickly exercise the runtime's variant fallthrough path when the preferred model is saturated, and measure end-to-end tail impact on p95/p99 and throughput. This is exploratory: keep runs short (5–10m) but with enough bursts to exercise fallbacks.

Hypotheses:
- H1: Fallthrough to a slightly smaller quantized variant will increase p99 by ~15–40% under bursty load due to context-switch overheads (kv cache miss + scheduling).
- H2: Routing logic (warm vs cold pool) will dominate short spikes — i.e., latency hit concentrated in first 30s of a burst.
- H3: Mixed arrival shapes (Poisson vs sawtooth) change effective throughput of fallback path because batching efficiency drops.

Environment:
- Cluster: ci-infer-us-west-2 (A10G-backed nodes)
- Models: redwood-v1-2048 (baseline), redwood-v1-2048-8bit (quant), redwood-v1-512 (compact), redwood-legacy-v0 (fallback)
- Serving config: continuous batching enabled, max_batch=32, batch_timeout_ms=8, prefetch_cache=enabled, kv_cache_size=4GB
- Client: loadgen-3 (golang), metrics via prometheus scrape (15s), traces sampled 1/200

Test matrix (short runs):
1) Poisson(λ=40 qps) steady 10m, prefer redwood-v1, capacity artificially constrained to saturate at 30qps (force fallthrough).
2) Sawtooth ramp 0→60 qps every 60s for 8 cycles, 8m total.
3) Bursty pulses: base 10 qps, every 30s inject 200 reqs at 1ms spacing (simulate microburst), 10m.
4) Control: same as 1) but no fallthrough (capacity sufficient) to capture baseline.

Quick raw observations (scratched during runs):
- 2025-01-12 10:03:05 run1 start: Immediately saw 10–12% increased p95 when first fallback occurred, p99 spike visible for ~45s after each fallback decision.
- KV cache: miss rate for fallback variant spiked to 78% on first minute after fallthrough, then stabilized ~22% (warm-up effect).
- CPU: host-side scheduling jitter increased on nodes hosting both primary and fallback; observed %steal spikes (kernel metrics) during pulse windows.

Aggregated summary (5m windows, run1 Poisson):
- Baseline (no fallthrough): p50=8ms, p95=26ms, p99=58ms, qps=29 (saturated target)
- With fallthrough: p50=10ms, p95=33ms, p99=87ms, qps=28.3 (slight drop)
- 95th delta ~+7ms (~27%), p99 delta +29ms (~50%)

Sawtooth (ramp cycles):
- Each ramp up triggered an initial p99 flash (200–500ms) for ~20–40s, correlated with cold fallback nodes spinning up new containers.
- When ramp down occurred, we saw an overshoot in queued requests (backlog ~120 reqs) causing a second p99 plateau; suggests teardown is asynchronous and aggressive scale-down hurts short-term tail.

Bursty pulses (microburst):
- Microburst injected during fallthrough causes p99 >1s in the worst case.
- Batching behaved poorly because fallback variant requests didn't batch with the primary variant requests (variant affinity in batcher). This increased per-token cost and latency.

Trace snippets (notes):
- Trace 0x7a3b: fallback decision at t0, client saw immediate 302ms RTT; server-side: queue->schedule->load-variant (60ms), kvcache-load (120ms), kernel-switch (80ms), generate (35ms). Key cost was kvcache load and variant load penalty.

Postmortem ideas / next actions (prioritized):
1) Introduce lightweight warm-handoff: keep 1 ephemeral worker per node pre-pulled with fallback variant to avoid variant-load penalty for first 20s. Quick experiment: can reduce initial p99 flash by ~2x in limited runs.
2) Improve batcher mixing policy: allow short-delay window (2–4ms) to mix requests across compatible variants (if quantization compatible) to preserve batching efficiency. Risk: slightly higher latency for all.
3) Tune scale-down grace period: increase from 10s to 40s to avoid teardown-induced backlogs seen on ramp down.
4) Add fast-path for KV cache priming: opportunistic async prefetch of per-tenant KV for likely fallback requests based on routing heuristics.

Hypothesis experiments (to schedule):
- H2b: Keep ephemeral fallback worker warm but CPU-limited; measure p99 reduction vs cost delta — run 3x 15m experiments.
- H3b: Test batcher mixing window 2ms vs 6ms under identical sawtooth pattern; measure token-level throughput and p95/p99 tradeoffs.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How often do real production tenants actually hit these fallthrough paths? We need production sampling approval to replay 1% of traffic.
- How does model size affect KV cache penalty? Preliminary suggests larger context models have larger priming costs (longer disk/mmap hits).
- Is there a safe heuristic for mixing quantized and FP variants without degrading generation quality? Requires eval set.

Quick cost note (back-of-envelope):
- Keeping 1 warm fallback worker per node increased hourly cost ~+8% in this test cluster, but reduced p99 flashes substantially. Need larger-scale cost simulation.

Notes to self: capture a couple of representative traces (IDs above) and attach to JIRA-ENG-4921. Add a simple dashboard: "variant-fallthrough-p99-flash" with two series (fallback_rate, p99).

Appendix (short run commands):
- loadgen client: ./loadgen --target http://gw.cluster/redwood/generate --qps 40 --dist poisson --duration 600 --headers "x-tenant:test-variant1"
- snapshot prometheus: curl -s 'http://prom/prometheus/api/v1/query?query=http_request_duration_seconds%7Broute="/generate"%7D'

Conclusion (scratch): fallthrough behavior is a measurable source of transient tail inflation. Short-term mitigations (warm ephemeral, grace on scale-down, micro-batcher tweak) look promising; need cost-vs-latency tradeoff experiments and a small canary in prod (1% traffic) to validate.

-- end of scratchpad --
